blocks.title: NP-complete
blocks.text: NP-complete problems are both in NP and as hard as the hardest problems in NP. If any NP-complete problem could be solved efficiently, every NP problem could be.

Example: the knapsack problem. A knapsack has a maximum weight capacity and each item has a weight and a value; the goal is the most valuable combination that does not exceed the capacity. Verifying a proposed set is easy (add the weights and values), but finding the best combination is hard because the number of combinations grows exponentially with the number of items, so brute force soon becomes impractical.

blocks.alt: Venn diagram: a large circle NP-Hard at the top overlaps a circle NP below it; the overlapping part is labelled NP-Complete. A small oval P sits inside NP at the bottom.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.4: Venn diagram of the complexity classes P, NP, NP-hard, and NP-complete (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.4).

blocks.text: Whether P equals NP is one of the most important unsolved problems in computer science, with major implications for cryptography, algorithm design and computational complexity (Did You Know).
